How Online Casino Loyalty Tiers and Comp Points Actually Work

Published November 11, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Every online casino wants you to notice the welcome bonus. Fewer players pay close attention to the loyalty program sitting quietly underneath it — the system of points, tiers, and comp cash that actually determines what a regular player gets back over months of play. A deposit bonus is a one-time event. A loyalty tier is closer to a running tab, and understanding how it's calculated tells you a lot more about your real long-run return than any sign-up offer does.

In this guide

  1. What comp points actually measure
  2. A worked example: turning play into points into cash
  3. Why tiers matter more than the points themselves

What comp points actually measure

Comp points (sometimes called tier credits, loyalty points, or reward points depending on the operator) are almost never based on how much you win or lose. They're based on theoretical loss — the amount the house edge says you'll lose on average given how much you wagered, regardless of what actually happened on any given session. A player who wagers $5,000 through a game with a 2% house edge has a theoretical loss of about $100, whether they personally finished that session up $300 or down $800. The casino's comp system is built around that $100 expected figure, not your actual result, because theoretical loss is the number the casino can predict and budget against — your actual swings are just noise around it.

This is also why comp earning is usually expressed as points per dollar wagered (handle), not points per dollar lost. A big winning session still earns a full load of points, because the casino is compensating you for the action you generated and the edge it expects to collect over time, not punishing or rewarding you based on a single outcome.

A worked example: turning play into points into cash

Say an online casino's slots program awards 1 point per $10 wagered, and points redeem at a rate of 100 points = $1 in comp cash. A player who wagers $3,000 over a month earns 300 points, worth $3 in comp cash — which sounds small because, on its own, it is. The number that actually matters is the rate of return relative to theoretical loss, not the raw dollar figure.

Why the multiplier matters more than the base rate: the base earn rate rarely changes much between casinos, but the tier multiplier can. Going from a base tier to a mid-level tier that pays 1.5× points on the exact same play turns a 2.5% comp return into a 3.75% comp return — a 50% improvement in what you get back, without changing a single thing about how or how much you played.

Why tiers matter more than the points themselves

The points-to-cash conversion rate is usually fixed and unremarkable. What actually moves the needle on a loyalty program's value is which tier a player sits in, because tiers typically unlock three things beyond a faster point multiplier: better comp redemption rates on the same points, perks that have real cash value but aren't labeled as "comps" (expedited withdrawals, dedicated account support, periodic free spins or bonus credits, invitations to higher-value promotions), and in some programs a cashback percentage on net losses that only kicks in above a certain tier. That last one is structurally different from standard comps — it's based on your actual result over a period, not theoretical loss — and it's usually the single most valuable perk reserved for a casino's top tiers.

Tiers are typically earned (and maintained) based on points accumulated within a rolling window — often a calendar year, or a trailing 30 or 90 days — rather than being permanent once reached. A player who qualifies for a mid-tier status in January but barely plays for the next several months can get quietly demoted at the next review period, which is worth knowing before treating a tier like a one-time achievement rather than something that needs ongoing play to maintain.

Why slots and table games don't earn points at the same rate

Most loyalty programs pay a noticeably lower point rate on blackjack, baccarat, and other low-house-edge table games than they do on slots, and the reason is directly tied to the theoretical-loss logic from earlier. A slot with a 4-6% house edge generates far more theoretical loss per dollar wagered than a blackjack table running close to 0.5% with correct strategy — so if a casino paid the same points-per-dollar-wagered rate across both, table game players would be earning comps wildly out of proportion to what they actually cost the house. Scaling the point rate down for low-edge games keeps comps roughly proportional to theoretical loss across every game in the casino, rather than accidentally handing out a far richer return to whoever happens to play the lowest-edge game available.

How this compares to a deposit bonus

A welcome bonus and a loyalty program solve different problems for the casino, which is why they're structured so differently. A deposit bonus is a one-time acquisition cost designed to get a new player to sign up and fund an account — it's generous on paper but usually comes with a wagering requirement that has to be cleared before any of it becomes withdrawable cash. A loyalty program, by contrast, is a retention mechanism built around the casino's long-run economics — it pays out slowly, in small increments, in exchange for continued play, and most of what it offers (comp cash, tier perks, occasional cashback) carries far lighter restrictions than bonus funds do, since it's compensating real wagering activity rather than functioning as promotional bait.

Reading the math before you chase a tier

The trap in any comp or loyalty system is treating the tier itself as the goal instead of a side effect of play you'd be doing anyway. Comp returns, even at a generous tier, are almost always a small single-digit percentage of theoretical loss — nowhere near enough to turn a losing game mathematically profitable, and nowhere near worth increasing your wagering specifically to reach the next status level. The programs are genuinely useful as a modest rebate on play you've already decided to do, the same way a cash-back credit card is useful on spending you were doing anyway, but they work against you the moment they start influencing how much or how fast you play. If you're tracking this kind of return alongside your overall bankroll, our guide on bankroll management for casino games covers how to think about that balance without letting a loyalty tier distort it.

Frequently asked questions

Do online casino comp points expire?

Often yes, though the terms vary widely by operator — some expire unused points after a set number of months of inactivity, while tier status itself commonly resets or downgrades at the end of a rolling evaluation period, separate from whether the points themselves expire.

Is it better to chase comp points or just play the lowest house-edge game available?

For your bankroll, the lowest house-edge game almost always wins — comp returns are typically a small fraction of theoretical loss, nowhere near enough to offset playing a higher-edge game just to earn points faster.

Why do table games earn comp points more slowly than slots?

Because comps are based on theoretical loss (house edge × amount wagered), and table games like blackjack typically carry a much lower house edge than slots. Scaling the point rate down for low-edge games keeps comps roughly proportional across every game rather than over-rewarding whoever plays the lowest-edge option.

Does winning or losing change how many comp points I earn?

Generally no. Standard comp points are earned on wagering volume (handle), not on your actual win or loss for a session, since they're built around the casino's expected edge rather than any single outcome.

Is top-tier cashback the same thing as a comp point?

No. Standard comps are based on theoretical loss regardless of your actual result, while cashback perks reserved for higher tiers are typically based on your actual net losses over a period — a different calculation that only pays out if you're genuinely down money for that window.
